comments.author: ardy42
comments.story: U.S. Gov Privacy Watchdog Under Pressure to Recommend Facial Recognition Ban
comments.why: Ex-CIA specialist on changing gait with a pebble in the shoe
comments.text: > Chinese ‘gait recognition’ tech IDs people by how they walk [LINK] An ex-CIA disguise specialist said that you can change your gait by putting a pebble in your shoe: [VIDEO] Her comments were targeting human recognition, and I speculate that one of the reasons she was allowed to share her disguise techniques is that maybe they're ineffective against automated facial recognition and therefore obsolete.

comments.author: ShorsHammer
comments.story: HK's extradition law: Not just HK people have reason to fear Chinese “justice”
comments.why: CIA video on disguising embassy-tasked staff
comments.text: Somewhat tangential: Do you think there are no spies operating in China whom are known to the current government? Why would China choose some random Westerners over known intel assets while knowing full well the case will appear so prominently on the world stage? Tourism makes up 10% of their economy. Nations tolerate this stuff and are well aware of who is who, it's how it is. Kicking out a known operative means another unknown will replace them. Better the enemy you know and such. There's a recent video from the CIA on the lengths they go to disguise embassy-tasked folk and how they get them out into the _world_. [VIDEO]

comments.author: eiaoa
comments.story: Singapore to test facial recognition on lampposts, stoking privacy fears
comments.why: Cited as example of intelligence disguise knowledge
comments.text: > Someone that does not want to be tracked by facial or gait recognition, either because he's a criminal or a political activist, will always be able to do that. There might be a race between the recognition software and the circumvention technology, but a dedicated individual will always be able to avoid that. One issue is disseminating the knowledge needed to defeat such systems. I'm sure the CIA and KGB have manuals and training programs to teach those skills [1], but I'm not sure if the information is publicly available in a readily accessible form (e.g. not spread in small pieces among 100 books).
